title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 875–876 (Night 207, continuing nights-206), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 207 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. As he studies the red stone in the light, a bird swoops down, snatches it from his hand and flies off; he runs after it from hill to hill until nightfall, and sleeps hungry and lost beneath the tree where it roosts. Each morning the bird flies on at just his pace, and he follows it for ten days, living on plants and stream water, until it vanishes into a thriving city. Resting by a stream outside, he remembers the ease and company he has lost, weeps, and recites a poem of three stanzas with a refrain; then he walks slowly into the city, and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّابِعَةُ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sābiʿatu baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the seventh after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and seventh night,
sentences.n: The night is numbered “the seventh after the two hundred”: al-sābiʿa, “the seventh”, is feminine to agree with layla. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّهُ لَمَّا أَخَذَ الْفَصَّ لِيُبْصِرَهُ فِى النُّورِ صَارَ يَتَأَمَّلُ فِيهِ وَهُوَ فِي يَدِهِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu annahu lammā akhadha al-faṣṣa li-yubṣirahu fī al-nūri ṣāra yataʾammalu fīhi wa-huwa fī yadihi
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that-he, when he-took the-stone to-see-it in the-light, began he-contemplates in-it, and-it (was) in his-hand.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when Qamar al-Zamān had taken the stone to look at it in the light, he began to study it closely as it lay in his hand.
sentences.n: The print has ليبصرة, a misprint for ليبصره, corrected here. li-yubṣirahu, “in order to see it”: li- with the subjunctive gives purpose, and the -hu is the stone. annahu, “that he”: the -hu stands for Qamar al-Zamān, picking the story up where the last night left it, with the red stone he had untied from Budūr's drawstring. ṣāra with an imperfect, “he began to …, he went on …”, a construction met constantly in this tale. taʾammala fī, Form V, “to look closely at, study”; the hamza of يتأمل is printed. wa-huwa fī yadihi, “while it was in his hand”: a circumstantial clause opened by wa-. The print spells fī both فى and في; both are kept.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِطَائِرٍ انْقَضَّ عَلَى قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ وَخَطَفَ الْفَصَّ مِنْ يَدِهِ وَطَارَبِهِ وَحَطَّ بِهِ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-ṭāʾirin inqaḍḍa ʿalā Qamari al-Zamāni wa-khaṭafa al-faṣṣa min yadihi wa-ṭāra bihi wa-ḥaṭṭa bihi ʿalā al-arḍi
sentences.l: And-behold, a-bird swooped upon Qamar al-Zamān, and-snatched the-stone from his-hand, and-flew with-it, and-alighted with-it upon the-ground.
sentences.i: And all at once a bird swooped down on Qamar al-Zamān, snatched the stone from his hand, flew off with it, and came down with it on the ground.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-, “and behold!”: idhā of surprise, with bi- marking what suddenly appears. inqaḍḍa ʿalā, Form VII, “to swoop down on”, of a bird of prey. The print runs ṭāra bihi, “it flew off with it”, together as one word, وطاربه; it is kept as set. In ṭāra bihi and ḥaṭṭa bihi, bi- is “with, carrying”. ḥaṭṭa, “to put down”; of a bird, “to alight”. The ئ of طائر is printed.

sentences.t: فَخَافَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ عَلَى الْفَصِّ وَجَرَى خَلْفَ الطَّائِرِ
sentences.tr: fa-khāfa Qamaru al-Zamāni ʿalā al-faṣṣi wa-jarā khalfa al-ṭāʾiri
sentences.l: And-feared Qamar al-Zamān for the-stone, and-ran behind the-bird.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān feared for the stone and ran after the bird.
sentences.n: khāfa ʿalā, “to fear for”: ʿalā marks what one fears for, as against khāfa min, “to be afraid of”. jarā, in the later language simply “to run”.

sentences.t: فَصَارَ الطَّائِرُ يَجْرِي عَلَى قَدْرِ جَرْيِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāra al-ṭāʾiru yajrī ʿalā qadri jaryi Qamari al-Zamāni
sentences.l: And-began the-bird runs according-to (the) measure (of the) running (of) Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.i: And the bird went on ahead of him at just the pace that Qamar al-Zamān ran.
sentences.n: ʿalā qadri, “according to the measure of, just as much as”. The bird too is said to “run”, yajrī: it keeps pace with him, never letting itself be caught and never losing him.

sentences.t: فَلَمْ يَزَلْ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ يَتْبَعُهُ مِنْ مَحَلٍّ إِلَى مَحَلٍّ وَمِنْ تَلٍّ إِلَى تَلٍّ إِلَى أَنْ دَخَلَ اللَّيْلُ وَأَظْلَمَ الْجَوُّفَنَامَ الطَّائِرُ عَلَى شَجَرَةٍ عَالِيَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lam yazal Qamaru al-Zamāni yatbaʿuhu min maḥallin ilā maḥallin wa-min tallin ilā tallin ilā an dakhala al-laylu wa-aẓlama al-jawwu fa-nāma al-ṭāʾiru ʿalā shajaratin ʿāliyatin
sentences.l: And-not ceased Qamar al-Zamān following-it from place to place and-from hill to hill, until that entered the-night and-grew-dark the-sky; and-slept the-bird upon a-tree high.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān kept following it from place to place and from hill to hill, until night came on and the sky grew dark, and the bird settled to sleep in a tall tree.
sentences.n: lam yazal with an imperfect, “he did not cease …, he kept on …”. ilā an, “until”, here with the perfect for what actually happened. jaww, “the air, the sky”. The print runs al-jawwu fa-nāma together as one word, الجوفنام; it is kept as set.

sentences.t: فَوَقَفَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ تَحْتَهَا وَصَارَ مُتَحَيِّرًا وَقَدْ سَاخَتْ رُوحُهُ مِنَ الْجُوعِ وَالتَّعَبِ
sentences.tr: fa-waqafa Qamaru al-Zamāni taḥtahā wa-ṣāra mutaḥayyiran wa-qad sākhat rūḥuhu mina al-jūʿi wa-al-taʿabi
sentences.l: And-stood Qamar al-Zamān beneath-it, and-became bewildered, and-had sunk his-soul from the-hunger and-the-weariness.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān stood beneath it at a loss what to do, his spirit sunk with hunger and weariness.
sentences.n: mutaḥayyir, “bewildered, at a loss”, active participle of Form V taḥayyara; after ṣāra it is accusative. sākhat rūḥuhu, literally “his soul sank”, as a foot sinks into soft ground: a Middle Arabic idiom for being utterly spent, ready to faint. Classical sākha is “to sink in, founder”. rūḥ, “soul”, is treated as feminine, as usual.

sentences.t: وَحَسَّ أَنَّهُ هَالِكٌ وَأَرَادَأَنْ يَرْجِعَ فَمَا عَرَفَ الْمَوْضِعَ الَّذِي جَاءَ مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: wa-ḥassa annahu hālikun wa-arāda an yarjiʿa fa-mā ʿarafa al-mawḍiʿa alladhī jāʾa minhu
sentences.l: And-he-felt that-he (was) perishing, and-he-wanted that he-return, but-not he-knew the-place which he-came from-it.
sentences.i: He felt that he was done for, and wanted to turn back, but he did not know the place he had come from.
sentences.n: ḥassa, “to feel, sense”, a by-form of the commoner aḥassa (Form IV), and the usual one in the later language; the shadda of وحسّ is printed. hālik, “perishing, as good as dead”. The print runs arāda an, “he wanted to”, together as one word, وارادان; it is kept as set. alladhī jāʾa minhu, “which he had come from”: the -hu of minhu returns to the place, as Arabic relative clauses require. The hamza of جاء is printed.

sentences.t: وَهَجَمَ عَلَيْهِ الظَّلَامُ فَقَالَ لَاحَوْلَ وَلَاقُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللّٰهِ الْعَلِيِّ الْعَظِيمِ
sentences.tr: wa-hajama ʿalayhi al-ẓalāmu fa-qāla lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-Allāhi al-ʿaliyyi al-ʿaẓīmi
sentences.l: And-rushed upon-him the-darkness, and-he-said: No might and-no strength except in-God, the-High, the-Mighty.
sentences.i: Darkness fell upon him, and he said, “There is no might and no strength save in God, the Exalted, the Mighty.”
sentences.n: hajama ʿalā, “to rush upon, fall upon”: the dark comes down on him like an attacker. lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-Allāh is the formula spoken in distress and helplessness; lā denying a whole class takes the accusative without tanwīn. The print sets lā ḥawla and wa-lā quwwata each as one word, لاحول and ولاقوة; they are kept as set.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَامَ تَحْتَ الشَّجَرَةِ الَّتِي فَوْقَهَا الطَّائِرُ إِلَى الصَّبَاحِ
sentences.tr: thumma nāma taḥta al-shajarati allatī fawqahā al-ṭāʾiru ilā al-ṣabāḥi
sentences.l: Then he-slept beneath the-tree which above-it (was) the-bird, until the-morning.
sentences.i: Then he slept until morning beneath the tree where the bird was perched.
sentences.n: allatī fawqahā al-ṭāʾiru, “which, above it, was the bird”: the -hā returns to the tree, as Arabic relative clauses require.

sentences.t: وَانْتَبَهَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ مِنْ نَوْمِهِ فَرَأَى الطَّائِرَ قَدِ انْتَبَهَ وَطَارَ مِنْ فَوْقِ الشَّجَرَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-intabaha Qamaru al-Zamāni min nawmihi fa-raʾā al-ṭāʾira qadi intabaha wa-ṭāra min fawqi al-shajarati
sentences.l: And-woke Qamar al-Zamān from his-sleep, and-he-saw the-bird had woken and-flown from above the-tree.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān woke from his sleep and saw that the bird had woken too and flown off from the top of the tree.
sentences.n: intabaha, Form VIII, “to wake, come to”. raʾā al-ṭāʾira qadi intabaha, “he saw the bird, it having woken”: the clause with qad describes the object. qadi takes a helping kasra before the joining alif of intabaha. The hamza of فرأى is printed.

sentences.t: فَمَشَى قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ خَلْفَهُ وَصَارَ ذٰلِكَ الطَّائِرُ يَطِيرُ قَلِيلًا بِقَدْرِ مَشْيِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-mashā Qamaru al-Zamāni khalfahu wa-ṣāra dhālika al-ṭāʾiru yaṭīru qalīlan bi-qadri mashyi Qamari al-Zamāni
sentences.l: And-walked Qamar al-Zamān behind-it, and-began that bird flies a-little, by-(the)-measure (of the) walking (of) Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān walked after it, and the bird flew on a little at a time, just as far as Qamar al-Zamān could walk.
sentences.n: bi-qadri, “by the measure of”, the same as ʿalā qadri above: bi- here is “according to”.

sentences.t: فَتَبَسَّمَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ وَقَالَ يَالَلّٰهِ الْعَجَبُ أَنَّ هٰذَا الطَّائِرَ كَانَ بِالْأَمْسِ يَطِيرُ بِقَدْرِ جَرْيَتِي وَفِي هٰذَا الْيَوْمِ عَلِمَ أَنِّي أَصْبَحْتُ تَعْبَانًا لَا أَقْدِرُ أَجْرِي فَصَارَ يَطِيرُ عَلَى قَدْرِ مَشْيَتِي
sentences.tr: fa-tabassama Qamaru al-Zamāni wa-qāla yā la-llāhi al-ʿajabu anna hādhā al-ṭāʾira kāna bi-al-amsi yaṭīru bi-qadri jaryatī wa-fī hādhā al-yawmi ʿalima annī aṣbaḥtu taʿbānan lā aqdiru ajrī fa-ṣāra yaṭīru ʿalā qadri mashyatī
sentences.l: And-smiled Qamar al-Zamān and-said: O for-God! The-wonder (is) that this bird was yesterday flying by-(the)-measure (of) my-running, and-on this day it-knew that-I have-become tired, not I-can I-run, so-it-began flies according-to (the) measure (of) my-walking.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān smiled and said, “Good God, how strange! Yesterday this bird flew just as fast as I ran, and today it knows that I am worn out and cannot run, so it flies only as fast as I walk.
sentences.n: yā la-llāhi, “O God!”, the cry of appeal and astonishment: the lām before the one appealed to takes a fatḥa. The print points يالَلّٰه itself and sets yā joined to it; both are kept. The full Classical phrase is yā la-llāhi li-al-ʿajabi, “O God, for the wonder!”; here al-ʿajabu stands on its own, and we read it as “the wonder is that …”, so the next word is vocalised anna. Reading inna, “truly”, opening a fresh sentence, is also possible. bi-al-amsi, “yesterday”. jaryatī and mashyatī, “my running”, “my walking”: Middle Arabic forms with the -a of a single act, where Classical would say jaryī and mashyī. taʿbān, “tired”, is a colloquial adjective of the faʿlān pattern for Classical taʿib; it is accusative after aṣbaḥtu. lā aqdiru ajrī, “I cannot run”: the second verb follows without an, as in the spoken language.

sentences.t: وَاللّٰهِ إِنَّ هٰذَا عَجِيبٌ
sentences.tr: wa-Allāhi inna hādhā ʿajībun
sentences.l: By-God, indeed this (is) wondrous!
sentences.i: By God, this is a marvel!
sentences.n: wa-Allāhi, “by God”: wa- here is the particle of oath.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنْ لَابُدَّ أَنْ أَتْبَعَ هٰذَا الطَّائِرَ فَإِمَّا أَنْ يَكُونَ هٰذَا الطَّائِرُ يَقُودُنِي لِحَيَوٰتِي أَوْ لِمَمَاتِي
sentences.tr: wa-lākin lā budda an atbaʿa hādhā al-ṭāʾira fa-immā an yakūna hādhā al-ṭāʾiru yaqūdunī li-ḥayātī aw li-mamātī
sentences.l: But no escape that I-follow this bird; for-either that is this bird leading-me to-my-life or to-my-death.
sentences.i: But I have no choice but to follow this bird: either it is leading me to my life or to my death.
sentences.n: lā budda an, “there is no escape from …, one must”; the print sets لابد as one word, kept. immā … aw, “either … or”. li-ḥayātī, li-mamātī, “to my life, to my death”: li- marks where he is led. The print spells ḥayāt the old way, حيوة, with a dagger alif over the wāw; it is kept. mamāt, “death”, chimes with it.

sentences.t: فَأَنَا أَتْبَعُهُ أَيْنَمَا يَتَوَجَّهُ لِأَنَّهُ عَلَى كُلِّ حَالٍ لَايُقِيمُ إِلَّا فِى الْبِلَادِ الْعَمَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-anā atbaʿuhu aynamā yatawajjahu li-annahu ʿalā kulli ḥālin lā yuqīmu illā fī al-bilādi al-ʿamāri
sentences.l: So-I, I-follow-it wherever it-turns, because-it in every case not stays except in the-lands the-inhabited.
sentences.i: So I will follow it wherever it goes; for whatever happens, it only settles in peopled country.”
sentences.n: aynamā, “wherever”: Classical puts the verb after it in the jussive, yatawajjah; the print's indicative yatawajjahu is the later usage. The print sets lā yuqīmu, “it does not stay”, as one word, لايقيم; it is kept. al-bilād al-ʿamār, “the inhabited lands”: a noun, ʿamār, “habitation, cultivation”, used as an adjective, a Middle Arabic turn for Classical al-bilād al-ʿāmira. The vowel is our reading; ʿimār, or ʿummār, “inhabitants”, are possible too. The thought: a bird does not live in empty waste, so it must lead him back among people.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ جَعَلَ يَمْشِي تَحْتَ الطَّائِرِ وَالطَّائِرُ يَبِيتُ فِي كُلِّ لَيْلَةٍ عَلَى شَجَرَةٍ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Qamara al-Zamāni jaʿala yamshī taḥta al-ṭāʾiri wa-al-ṭāʾiru yabītu fī kulli laylatin ʿalā shajaratin
sentences.l: Then indeed Qamar al-Zamān began walks beneath the-bird, and-the-bird spends-the-night in every night upon a-tree.
sentences.i: Then Qamar al-Zamān went walking along beneath the bird, and every night the bird roosted in a tree.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then”, a storyteller's transition; inna puts Qamar al-Zamān in the accusative. jaʿala with an imperfect, “he set about …”, like ṣāra. bāta, yabītu, “to spend the night”.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَلْ تَابِعَهُ مُدَّةَ عَشَرَةِ أَيَّامٍ وَقَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ يَتَقَوَّتُ مِنْ نَبَاتِ الْأَرْضِ وَيَشْرَبُ مِنْ أَنْهَارِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazal tābiʿahu muddata ʿasharati ayyāmin wa-Qamaru al-Zamāni yataqawwatu min nabāti al-arḍi wa-yashrabu min anhārihā
sentences.l: And-not he-ceased following-it (for a) period (of) ten days, while-Qamar al-Zamān feeds-himself from (the) plants (of) the-earth and-drinks from its-rivers.
sentences.i: He followed it for ten days, living on the plants of the earth and drinking from its streams.
sentences.n: lam yazal tābiʿahu: the predicate of zāla is accusative. muddata, “for a period of”, accusative of time. ʿashara, “ten”, takes the feminine-looking form before a masculine plural, ayyām, “days”. taqawwata min, Form V, “to feed oneself on, live on”, from qūt, “food, sustenance”; the shadda of يتقوّت is printed.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ عَشَرَةِ أَيَّامٍ أَشْرَفَ عَلَى مَدِينَةٍ عَامِرَةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda ʿasharati ayyāmin ashrafa ʿalā madīnatin ʿāmiratin
sentences.l: And-after ten days he-overlooked upon a-city flourishing.
sentences.i: And after ten days he came in sight of a thriving city.
sentences.n: ashrafa ʿalā, Form IV, “to look down on, come within sight of”, as from a height. ʿāmira, “inhabited, flourishing”.

sentences.t: فَمَرَقَ الطَّائِرُ مِثْلَ لَمْحِ الْبَصَرِ وَدَخَلَ تِلْكَ الْمَدِينَةَ وَغَابَ عَنْ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-maraqa al-ṭāʾiru mithla lamḥi al-baṣari wa-dakhala tilka al-madīnata wa-ghāba ʿan Qamari al-Zamāni
sentences.l: And-shot-off the-bird like (the) glance (of) the-eye, and-entered that city, and-vanished from Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.i: Then the bird shot off, quick as the twinkling of an eye, into that city, and was lost to Qamar al-Zamān's sight.
sentences.n: maraqa is Classically “to pass right through” its target, of an arrow; in the later language simply “to dart away, pass swiftly”. lamḥ al-baṣar, “the glance of the eye”, a stock phrase for an instant.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَعْرِفْ خَبَرَهُ وَلَا يَعْلَمُ أَيْنَ ذَهَبَ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yaʿrif khabarahu wa-lā yaʿlamu ayna dhahaba
sentences.l: And-not he-knew its-news, and-not he-knows where it-went.
sentences.i: He had no word of it, nor did he know where it had gone.
sentences.n: The two negations differ: lam with the jussive, lam yaʿrif, “he did not know”, for the past, and lā with the indicative, lā yaʿlamu, “he does not know”, for the lasting state.

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ وَقَالَ الْحَمْدُ لِلّٰهِ الَّذِي سَلَّمَنِي حَتَّى وَصَلْتُ إِلَى هٰذِهِ الْمَدِينَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjaba Qamaru al-Zamāni wa-qāla al-ḥamdu li-llāhi alladhī sallamanī ḥattā waṣaltu ilā hādhihi al-madīnati
sentences.l: And-wondered Qamar al-Zamān and-said: The-praise (be) to-God, who kept-me-safe until I-arrived at this city.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān marvelled at this and said, “Praise be to God, who has kept me safe until I reached this city!”
sentences.n: sallama, Form II, “to keep safe, bring through unharmed”. waṣala ilā, “to arrive at, reach”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ جَلَسَ عَلَى نَهْرٍ وَغَسَلَ يَدَيْهِ وَرِجْلَيْهِ وَوَجْهَهُ وَاسْتَرَاحَ سَاعَةً
sentences.tr: thumma jalasa ʿalā nahrin wa-ghasala yadayhi wa-rijlayhi wa-wajhahu wa-istarāḥa sāʿatan
sentences.l: Then he-sat upon a-river, and-washed his-two-hands and-his-two-feet and-his-face, and-rested an-hour.
sentences.i: Then he sat down by a stream, washed his hands, his feet and his face, and rested a while.
sentences.n: jalasa ʿalā nahrin, “sat by a river”: ʿalā is “at the edge of”. yadayhi, rijlayhi, duals, “his two hands, his two feet”. istarāḥa, Form X, “to rest”. sāʿa, “an hour”, in narrative often just “a while”.

sentences.t: فَتَذَكَّرَ مَا كَانَ فِيهِ مِنَ الرَّاحَةِ وَالْهَنَا وَاجْتِمَاعِ الشَّمْلِ
sentences.tr: fa-tadhakkara mā kāna fīhi mina al-rāḥati wa-al-hanā wa-ijtimāʿi al-shamli
sentences.l: And-he-remembered what he-was in-it of the-ease and-the-contentment and-(the)-gathering (of) the-scattered-company.
sentences.i: And he remembered the ease and contentment he had lived in, with all his dear ones gathered about him.
sentences.n: hanā, “contentment, well-being”, is Classical hanāʾ with the final hamza dropped, as in the spoken language. ijtimāʿ al-shaml, “the gathering of the scattered”: shaml is one's people and affairs held together, and the phrase means a family united.

sentences.t: وَنَظَرَ إِلَى مَا هُوَ فِيهِ مِنَ التَّعَبِ وَالْهَمِّ وَالْغُرْبَةِ وَالْجُوعِ وَالْفُرْقَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-naẓara ilā mā huwa fīhi mina al-taʿabi wa-al-hammi wa-al-ghurbati wa-al-jūʿi wa-al-furqati
sentences.l: And-he-looked to what he (is) in-it of the-weariness and-the-care and-the-exile and-the-hunger and-the-separation.
sentences.i: Then he looked at what he was in now: weariness and care, exile, hunger and separation.
sentences.n: mā kāna fīhi … mā huwa fīhi, “what he had been in … what he is in”: the two lists set past and present against each other. ghurba, “being a stranger in a foreign land”. furqa, “separation” from those one loves. The shadda of والهمّ is printed.

sentences.t: فَفَاضَتْ دُمُوعُهُ وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-fāḍat dumūʿuhu wa-anshada yaqūlu
sentences.l: And-overflowed his-tears, and-he-recited, saying:
sentences.i: His tears brimmed over, and he recited:
sentences.n: anshada yaqūlu, “he recited, saying”, the stock formula that brings on verse.

sentences.t:
اَخْفَيْتُ مَا الْقَاهُ مِنْكَ وَقَدْ ظَهَر * وَالنَّوْمُ مِنْ عَيْنِي تَبَدَّلَ بِالسَّهَر
نَادَيْتُ لَمَّا اَوْهَنَتْ قَلْبِي الْفِكَر * يَا دَهْرُ لَا تُبْقِي عَلَيَّ وَلَا تَذَر
هَا مُهْجَتِي بَيْنَ الْمَشَقَّةِ وَالْخَطَر
لَوْكَانَ سُلْطَانُ الْمَحَبَّةِ مُنْصِفِي * مَا كَانَ نَوْمِي مِنْ عُيُونِي قَدْ نُفِي
يَا سَادَتِي رِفْقًا لِصَبٍّ مُدْنِفٍ * وَتَعَطَّفُوا لعَزِيزِ قَوْمٍ ذَلَّ فِي
شَرْعِ الْهَوَى وَغَنِيِّ قَوْمٍ اِفْتَقَر
لَحَّ الْعَوَاذِلُ فِيْكَ مَا طَاوَعْتُهُمْ * وَسَدَدْتُ كُلَّ مَسَامِعِي وَصَمَمْتُهُمْ
قَالُوا عَشِقْتَ مُهَفْهَفًا فَاَجَبْتُهُمْ * اِخْتَرْتُهُ مِنْ بَيْنِهِمْ وَتَرَكْتُهُمْ
كُفُّوا اِذَا وَقَعَ الْقَضَا عَمِيَ الْبَصَر
sentences.tr:
akhfaytu mā alqāhu minka wa-qad ẓahar * wa-al-nawmu min ʿaynī tabaddala bi-al-sahar
nādaytu lammā awhanat qalbī al-fikar * yā dahru lā tubqī ʿalayya wa-lā tadhar
hā muhjatī bayna al-mashaqqati wa-al-khaṭar
law kāna sulṭānu al-maḥabbati munṣifī * mā kāna nawmī min ʿuyūnī qad nufī
yā sādatī rifqan li-ṣabbin mudnifin * wa-taʿaṭṭafū li-ʿazīzi qawmin dhalla fī
sharʿi al-hawā wa-ghaniyyi qawmin iftaqar
laḥḥa al-ʿawādhilu fīka mā ṭāwaʿtuhum * wa-sadadtu kulla masāmiʿī wa-ṣamamtuhum
qālū ʿashiqta muhafhafan fa-ajabtuhum * ikhtartuhu min baynihim wa-taraktuhum
kuffū idhā waqaʿa al-qaḍā ʿamiya al-baṣar
sentences.l:
I-hid what I-meet-it from-you, and-(yet) it-has-appeared; * and-the-sleep from my-eye has-been-exchanged for-the-wakefulness.
I-called, when had-weakened my-heart the-thoughts: * O Time, not you-spare upon-me and-not you-leave!
Lo, my-heart's-blood (is) between the-hardship and-the-peril.
If were (the) sultan (of) the-love fair-to-me, * not would-be my-sleep from my-eyes already banished.
O my-masters, gentleness to-a-lover wasted-by-sickness, * and-be-kind to-(the)-mighty-one (of) a-people (who) became-low in
(the) law (of) the-passion, and-(the)-rich-one (of) a-people (who) became-poor.
Persisted the-blamers about-you; not I-obeyed-them, * and-I-stopped all my-ears and-I-was-deaf-to-them.
They-said: You-have-loved a-slender-waisted-one; and-I-answered-them: * I-chose-him from among-them, and-I-left-them.
Desist! When falls the-decree, goes-blind the-sight.
sentences.i:
I hid what I suffer from you, yet it has come to light, * and sleep has left my eyes and turned to waking.
When my thoughts had worn my heart down, I cried, * “O Time, you spare me nothing and leave me nothing!”
See, my life hangs between hardship and danger.
Were the sultan of love but fair to me, * sleep would not have been banished from my eyes.
My masters, be gentle with a lover sick to wasting, * and pity one mighty among his people, brought low by
the law of passion, one rich among his people, now made poor.
The blamers pressed me about you; I did not heed them, * I stopped my ears and turned deaf to them.
They said, “You love one slender of waist”; I answered them, * “I chose him from among them all, and left the rest.”
Enough! When fate comes down, the eyes go blind.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed; only يا in the second line, which the print leaves bare, is pointed by us. The form is strophic, in the manner of a muwashshaḥ or mukhammas: three stanzas, each of two couplets followed by a single short line. The couplets of the first stanza rhyme in -ar (ẓahar, sahar, fikar, tadhar), those of the second in -fī (munṣifī, nufī, mudnif(in), fī), those of the third in -tuhum; each stanza closes with its short line returning to the refrain rhyme in -ar (khaṭar, iftaqar, baṣar). In the second stanza the sense runs on from one printed line into the next: dhalla fī / sharʿi al-hawā, “brought low in the law of passion”. lā tubqī … wa-lā tadhar echoes the Qurʾān (74:28), said there of Hell, “it spares not and leaves not”; the print's tubqī is indicative, a statement rather than a command. The close of the second stanza echoes the saying irḥamū ʿazīza qawmin dhalla wa-ghaniyya qawmin iftaqara, “pity the mighty man of a people who is brought low, and the rich man of a people who is made poor”. The print leaves the lām of لعَزِيزِ without its kasra, and sets law kāna as one word, لَوْكَانَ; both are kept. ṣabb, “a lover pining with passion”; mudnif, “wasted by lingering sickness”. laḥḥa, “to persist, press”, more often alaḥḥa in Classical. ṣamamtuhum, “I was deaf to them”, if -hum is the blamers; if it is the ears, “I stopped them up”: the reading is doubtful. muhafhaf, “slender, slim-waisted”, a stock epithet of the beloved. al-qaḍā is qaḍāʾ, “the divine decree, fate”, with the hamza dropped, as the print sets it. The print sets a bare alif without hamza in اَخْفَيْتُ, الْقَاهُ, اَوْهَنَتْ, فَاَجَبْتُهُمْ and اِذَا, and points fīka as فِيْكَ; all are kept.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ لَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ وَاسْتَرَاحَ قَامَ يَمْشِي قَلِيلًا قَلِيلًا حَتَّى دَخَلَ الْمَدِينَةَ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Qamara al-Zamāni lammā faragha min shiʿrihi wa-istarāḥa qāma yamshī qalīlan qalīlan ḥattā dakhala al-madīnata
sentences.l: Then indeed Qamar al-Zamān, when he-finished from his-verse and-rested, rose walking little little, until he-entered the-city.
sentences.i: Then, when Qamar al-Zamān had finished his verses and rested, he got up and walked on, little by little, until he entered the city.
sentences.n: faragha min, “to be done with, finish”. qāma yamshī, “he rose, walking”: qāma with an imperfect is “he set off doing”. qalīlan qalīlan, “little by little”: the repeated accusative gives gradual progress.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ. The print sets the name as one word here, شهرزاد.
